classification.difficultyReason: Students construct sketches from equations using the specified intercept, asymptote and point. The hardest part combines a negative exponent, external negative sign and vertical shift, requiring coordination of increasing behaviour, position below the asymptote and approach to it on the right.

content.prompt:
Sketch these exponential equations.
Clearly label the $y$-intercept, asymptote, and the point where $x = 1$.

answer.worked:
At $x=0$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=3^0+2\\y&=3\end{align*}$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,3)$. The asymptote is $y=2$.
At $x=1$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=3^1+2\\y&=5\end{align*}$$
Plot $(0,3)$ and $(1,5)$. Draw an increasing exponential curve above $y=2$, approaching the asymptote to the left.

spec.description: Increasing exponential with arrowheads at both curve ends, unticked axes, no point markers, and a dashed asymptote.
spec.answerVisibility: Answer only; the student receives an ungridded drawing region.

answer.worked:
At $x=0$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=-3^0-4\\y&=-5\end{align*}$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,-5)$. The asymptote is $y=-4$.
At $x=1$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=-3^{-1}-4\\y&=-\frac13-4\\y&=-\frac{13}{3}\end{align*}$$
Plot $(0,-5)$ and $(1,-\frac{13}{3})$. Draw an increasing exponential curve below $y=-4$, approaching the asymptote to the right.

At $x=0$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=2^0+3\\y&=4\end{align*}$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,4)$. The asymptote is $y=3$.
At $x=1$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=2^{-1}+3\\y&=\frac12+3\\y&=\frac72\end{align*}$$
Plot $(0,4)$ and $(1,\frac72)$. Draw a decreasing exponential curve above $y=3$, approaching the asymptote to the right.
